title: Thesis Defense: Discovering and Removing Latent Failure Modes in Neural Networks
description: Thesis Defense: Discovering and Removing Latent Failure Modes in Neural Networks Abstract: This thesis explores a particular class of neural network failure modes we call latent failure modes. Such failure modes are characterized by being hard to discover for the first time, but easy to reproduce once discovered. Examples of latent failure modes include adversarial examples for image models, jailbreaks and prompt injections for large language models (LLMs), and undesired backdoor behaviors purposefully inserted into the weights of models.     Our exploration of latent failure modes is based on a series of 5 case studies spanning the domains of game-playing, language modeling, and vision. Through these case studies we develop a number of important insights about latent failure modes, including that (a) even very capable AI systems can harbor serious naturally-ocurring latent failure modes; (b) across multiple domains, a promising strategy for finding latent failure modes is to train other AI systems to help find them; (c) a lack of high-quality, easy-to-use benchmarks is holding back progress in discovering and defending against latent failure modes in LLMs; and (d) the version of adversarial robustness most relevant to real-world systems (and the general problem of latent failure modes) is unrestricted adversarial robustness, which, despite receiving relatively little attention, may be more tractable than previously thought.      Taken together, our case studies advance the following conclusion: Although latent failure modes are a pervasive feature of modern AI systems that have resisted a decade of research into removing them, several neglected approaches to discovering and removing them could, with greater investment, substantially improve our ability to build reliable AI systems.  TBD October 20, 2026 HCI Seminar - Natasha Singer - How Big Tech Captured the Classroom and What We Can Do About It Natasha Singer New York Times Part Of HCI Seminar 2026-2027 4:00 P - 5:00 P Location 32-D463

title: CSAIL FORUM with Daniel Jackson: The Key to Agentic Software Development
description: CSAIL FORUM with Daniel Jackson: The Key to Agentic Software Development Abstract: AI-driven coding agents have opened a new world for building software. But applied in standard ways they are likely to just create a mountain of technical and cognitive debt. How do you take control and produce reliable and maintainable software? This talk, directed both at those who build software and those who are accountable for it, will explain how.Bio:Daniel Jackson is professor of computer science at MIT, and associate director of CSAIL. For his research in software, he won the ACM SIGSOFT Impact Award, the ACM SIGSOFT Outstanding Research Award and was made an ACM Fellow.He is the lead designer of the Alloy modeling language, and author of Software Abstractions. He chaired a National Academies study on software dependability, and has collaborated on software projects with NASA on air-traffic control, with Massachusetts General Hospital on proton therapy, and with Toyota on autonomous cars.His most recent book, Essence of Software, offers a fresh approach to software design, and shows how thinking about software in terms of concepts and their relationships can lead to more usable and effective software.
